Submitted electronically to: www.regulations.gov 
 
June 15, 2026 
 
Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS–0062–P, Mail Stop C4–26–05 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244–1850 
  
Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage 
Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified 
Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges [CMS–0062–P] 
  
Administrator Oz, 
  
The National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA) appreciates the opportunity to provide 
comments to CMS on its proposed rule: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection 
and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for 
Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and 
Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges. 
 
NCPA represents America’s community pharmacists, including 18,900 independent community 
pharmacies. Almost half of all community pharmacies provide long-term care services and play a 
critical role in ensuring patients have immediate access to medications in both community and 
long-term care (LTC) settings. Together, our members employ 235,000 individuals, and provide 
an expanding set of healthcare services to millions of patients every day. Our members are small 
business owners who are among America’s most accessible healthcare providers. NCPA submits 
these comments on behalf of both community and LTC independent pharmacies. 
 
CMS is proposing to require state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care 
plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs to support the NCPDP Formulary 
and Benefit (F&B) standard version 60 adopted by the Secretary in 45 CFR 170.205(u), for 
transmitting formulary and benefit information between providers and impacted payers, and 
NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standard version 13 adopted by the Secretary in 45 
CFR 170.205(c), to enable real-time, patient-specific prescription benefit information to be 
2 of 8 
 
delivered to providers at the point of prescribing.1 NCPA supports this proposal. We encourage 
CMS and ONC to stay aligned on listening conversations on how to improve RTPB moving 
forward, and applaud the agencies’ stakeholder listening efforts to date. 
NCPA also supports CMS’ announcement to pledge to advance electronic prior authorization 
beyond minimum compliance requirements by implementing interoperable, end-to-end 
workflows across medical prior authorization processes, and its stated commitment to working 
collectively across stakeholders to support alignment, seamless data exchange, and 
measurable improvements across medical prior authorization workflows consistent with CMS-
0057-F.2 However, NCPA notes that this pledge only applies to electronic prior authorization for 
medical benefit and services only, and does not include drugs, since CMS is currently working to 
finalize the proposed rule. 
 
Updated Version Adoption  
NCPA supports CMS’ current approach with the versions proposed and advises CMS to not 
name versions of NCPDP standards beyond those proposed in this rule; specifically, that the 
final rule name no version newer than NCPDP SCRIPT Standard Version 2023011© (as codified 
at 45 CFR 170.205(b)), NCPDP Formulary & Benefit Standard Version 60 (as codified at 45 CFR 
170.205(u)), and NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard Version 13 (as codified at 45 
CFR 170.205(c)).  The industry is in active transition to the currently proposed versions and is not 
prepared for a subsequent version mandate.   
The standards named in this proposed rule were finalized for Part D purposes in the Medicare 
Part D e-prescribing standards final rule published in June 2024, with compliance dates of January 
1, 2027 (F&B v60, RTPB v13) and January 1, 2028 (SCRIPT 2023011©). Pharmacies and other 
stakeholders are currently in the process of implementing these transitions. The Part D 
compliance deadlines are imminent, and the impacted payers newly brought into scope under 
CMS-0062-P (Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP issuers) are only now beginning implementation planning. 
Requiring newer versions of any of these three standards in the final rule would result in 
significant administrative burden and cost to pharmacies and other stakeholders. 
Implementation Considerations and Timeline  
NCPDP, as the ANSI-accredited standards development organization responsible for the NCPDP 
SCRIPT, RTPB, and Formulary and Benefit standards, has previously communicated minimum 
implementation timeline recommendations to CMS that are directly relevant to this rulemaking 
 
1 See Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and 
Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State 
Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and 
Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges. Fed Reg Vol 91, No 71 (April 14, 2026), at 
20033. 
2 See Additional Use Case – Electronic Prior Authorization | CMS. 
3 of 8 
 
and that CMS should treat as a floor, not a ceiling, when establishing compliance dates for the 
pharmacy benefit prior authorization requirements proposed in CMS-0062-P.   
The requirements proposed in CMS-0062-P present a significant challenge. For the majority 
of impacted payers outside the Medicare Part D context, including State Medicaid and CHIP Fee-
for-Service (FFS) programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP 
issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchange (FFEs), supporting NCPDP SCRIPT ePA transactions 
for pharmacy benefit drugs is net-new functionality. There is no existing infrastructure to update; 
it must be built which means new system integrations, new trading partner onboarding, new 
testing protocols, new staff training, and new operational procedures; all of which must be 
coordinated across a fragmented multi-vendor ecosystem. This is a fundamentally larger 
undertaking than what NCPDP's 24-month minimum was designed to address.  Accordingly, 
NCPA urges CMS to extend the proposed October 1, 2027 compliance date for the pharmacy 
benefit requirements to no earlier than 24 months from the effective date of the final rule, 
consistent with NCPDP's own stated minimum for a version transition.    
Additionally, a later implementation timeline aligning with the suggested 24 month minimum, 
allows 
the 
industry 
time 
to comply with other 
HHS/CMS 
transaction 
mandates, 
including the NCPDP 
Telecommunication Standard 
(April 14, 2028, per CMS-0056-F), 
and the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard (January 1, 2028). This later implementation timeline will also 
negate the need for compliance with the 2017071 version of the SCRIPT Standard, which is 
transitioning to the 2023011© version as of January 1, 2028.   
CMS proposes two electronic prior authorization pathways for drugs, FHIR-based APIs for medical 
benefit drugs and NCPDP standards for pharmacy benefit drugs. That said, to reduce 
administrative burden, NCPA encourages CMS to clarify or strengthen policy and implementation 
expectations in the following areas: 
 
Implementation Concerns for Workflow 
While federal programs accelerated adoption of EHRs and interoperability capabilities among 
many traditional provider settings, pharmacies were largely excluded from these incentives. As a 
result, pharmacists are increasingly participating in clinical, documentation-driven workflows 
without the same level of support.  
 
CMS’ proposed rule operationalizes drug prior authorization through two distinct electronic 
pathways tied to benefit type, which impacts pharmacists. The success of CMS’ approach 
depends on whether stakeholders including pharmacists can determine which pathway applies, 
and whether the system response is actionable in real workflows.  
 
 
 
4 of 8 
 
Clarifying Pathway and Workflow (Medical vs. Pharmacy Benefit) 
The proposed rule establishes two distinct electronic pathways depending on how a drug is 
covered: FHIR-based prior authorization APIs for medical benefit drugs (using the Da Vinci 
implementation guides) and NCPDP standards (SCRIPT ePA, F&B, RTPB) for pharmacy benefit 
drugs. NCPA encourages CMS to clarify expectations for how impacted payers will support 
identification of the correct authorization pathway and ensure actionable responses regardless 
of initiating actor, including pharmacists.  
 
NCPA also encourages CMS to clarify expectations for what constitutes an actionable response 
within prior authorization workflows. In practice, responses that indicate coverage 
requirements but do not clearly identify next steps will result in additional interpretation, 
submissions, delays, and administrative burden. NCPA further encourages CMS to further clarify 
how the market is expected to operationalize these two pathways to reduce administrative 
burden. 
 
This challenge also highlights the emerging need for greater workflow orchestration across prior 
authorization processes. These orchestration approaches are particularly relevant in scenarios 
where pharmacists, providers, and care teams must coordinate across systems to complete prior 
authorization-related tasks without duplicative or misrouted requests. Current industry efforts 
reflect a growing need to better coordinate medication-level data, coverage requirements, and 
authorization workflows across actors and systems. As these efforts mature, they may inform 
how prior authorization workflows are orchestrated end-to-end across FHIR and NCPDP-based 
processes, reducing fragmentation and improving routing accuracy across benefit types. 
 
Absent additional clarity, there is risk that organizations implement parallel and uncoordinated 
workflows across FHIR and NCPDP standards raising administrative burden rather than 
reducing it.  Without further clarification, there is risk that organizations implement 
disconnected solutions that increase administrative burden. 
 
Integrating Transactions and Workflow (NCPDP + Real-Time) 
NCPA recognizes NCPDP standards as essential and widely adopted transaction standards in the 
pharmacy ecosystem and supports continued alignment across standards to enable scalable 
implementation.  
 
CMS is explicitly seeking comment on questions that relate to this practical trade space, including 
questions about NCPDP Formulary & Benefit and RTPB (e.g., how data is made available, update 
frequency, lag, accuracy, and whether requiring multiple mechanisms adds value or burden).  
NCPA encourages CMS to use this rulemaking to clarify expectations for how impacted payers 
and market participants should support actionable, patient-specific benefit information in 
workflows, while recognizing that plan-level files and real-time responses are not operationally 
interchangeable today. Real-time responses must use adjudication processes that result in the 
same patient cost-sharing or utilization management determination as pharmacy claims. 
 
 
 
5 of 8 
 
Prior Authorization Timeframes and the Operational “Clock”  
CMS proposes to align and clarify PA decision timeframes for drugs across programs and expands 
transparency and reporting expectations. NCPA supports the intent of consistent and 
transparent timeframes, and encourages CMS to address the key operational question raised 
across the ecosystem: When does the PA clock start and stop?  
 
NCPA encourages CMS to consider whether additional specificity is needed to promote 
consistent measurement and avoid unintended consequences, including: 
• 
When a request is considered “received” for purposes of initiating the clock; 
• 
Whether (and how) a request is considered “complete”; and 
• 
How iterative workflows (requests for additional information, corrected submissions, 
re-routing between pathways) are treated in timeframe calculations and reporting.  
Without greater clarity, timeframes and public reporting risk not achieving true operational 
performance and may inadvertently shift accountability to downstream actors like pharmacists 
who do not control documentation completeness.  
 
NCPA also notes that prior authorization workflows extend beyond initial determination and 
include downstream processes such as appeals and peer-to-peer reviews. In current practice, 
these processes are often fragmented, inconsistently sequenced, and not well integrated into 
electronic workflows, resulting in delays and confusion regarding roles and timelines.  
 
NCPA encourages CMS to consider whether future policy or guidance should address how these 
processes can be more consistently defined and, where appropriate, supported through 
interoperable, electronic mechanisms, including patient driven data and interoperability. 
 
Pharmacists’ Dual Role in Care Delivery 
To ensure success of CMS’ proposal, CMS should recognize that pharmacists operate in a dual 
role within today’s healthcare system: 
1. Dispenser role: Pharmacists are downstream from prescribing providers and typically do 
not control the creation, completeness, or timing of clinical documentation required to 
support coverage determinations.  
2. Provider role (clinical services): Pharmacists are increasingly providing clinical services 
within scope of practice (e.g., medication management, chronic disease support, other 
billable interventions). In these cases, the pharmacist is the rendering provider and is 
directly responsible for the generation, management, and submission of clinical 
documentation necessary to support coverage and payment.  
Due to the pharmacist’s dual role, CMS policy should not assume pharmacists serve a single, static 
function, but should instead account for when pharmacists depend on external provider 
documentation and situations where pharmacists are the provider of record generating and 
submitting documentation.  
 
6 of 8 
 
Real-Time, Actionable Information at the Point of Care (Including Pharmacists) 
NCPA agrees that real-time access to benefit and coverage information can reduce unnecessary 
prior authorization and improve prescribing decisions. To be effective, however, information 
must be:  
 
• Available to all relevant participants in the care process, including pharmacists; 
• 
Presented in a way that is actionable within existing workflows; and 
• 
Paired with clear pathways for next steps, including initiation of prior authorization 
when required  
NCPA encourages CMS to reinforce that the purpose of modernizing electronic PA and real-time 
benefit is not merely to create endpoints, it is to enable workflow outcomes that reduce 
administrative burden. 
 
Patient Access and Participation in Prior Authorization Workflows 
CMS’ proposal expands expectations for data made available through APIs (including PA status 
and related information) and seeks input on consumer-facing capabilities. NCPA encourages CMS 
to reinforce that these capabilities should support not only access to information, but also 
meaningful understanding and usability of that information within the context of prior 
authorization workflows. NCPA encourages CMS to consider policy and guidance to support 
patient visibility, and also appropriate patient participation in prior authorization workflows. 
 
At the same time, NCPA encourages CMS to carefully consider implementation approaches that 
do not inadvertently introduce additional administrative burden.  
 
Explicit Responses to CMS Requests for Information (RFIs) 
NCPA appreciates CMS’s use of Requests for Information to inform future policy direction, and 
provides the following thoughts below: 
 
RFI 1: Electronic Event Notifications for Value-Based Care and Care Coordination (including 
ADTs) 
CMS seeks input on expanding and improving admission, discharge, and transfer (ADT) 
notifications and broader event notification capabilities, including which entity types should 
receive notifications and technical approaches. NCPA encourages CMS to explicitly consider 
pharmacist-enabled care coordination as part of these discussions, given pharmacists’ 
increasing role in medication management and transitions of care. 
 
RFI 2: Increasing Health Care Resiliency and Securing Health Care Operations 
CMS seeks feedback on cybersecurity, operational continuity, and modernizing secure exchange 
infrastructure. NCPA supports approaches that strengthen security and resiliency, while 
advising that CMS should recognize that smaller organizations like community pharmacies may 
not have the same infrastructure capabilities as large health systems.  
 
7 of 8 
 
RFI 3: Improving Payer API Technology Through Testing and Certification 
CMS explores stronger oversight and conformance mechanisms for payer APIs, including testing 
frameworks and certification models. NCPA encourages CMS to consider mechanisms, beyond 
API availability alone, that improve consistency, usability, ensuring that responses are 
actionable and support workflow integration between pharmacists and others.  
 
RFI 4: Using Technology to Manage Step Therapy 
NCPA appreciates CMS’s interest in improving step therapy processes. Step therapy policies are 
often a vehicle by PBMs and plans to force patients to repeat previously unsuccessful therapies 
after switching plans or coverage. Pharmacies help identify problems caused by step therapy, as 
they can often see a patient’s medication and treatment history. 
 
CMS can help reform step therapy by: 
• 
Supporting data exchange mechanisms that enable payers to access and recognize prior 
step therapy history; 
• 
Leveraging existing interoperability frameworks, including Payer-to-Payer APIs, to 
facilitate portability of medication and utilization management history; and 
• 
Encouraging standardization of step therapy documentation to reduce variability across 
payers. 
RFI 5: Prior Authorization Requirements for Laboratory Tests and DMEPOS Items 
CMS requests information about operational and patient access issues related to prior 
authorization for laboratory tests and DMEPOS items, including workflow delays and challenges 
when certain actors cannot directly initiate PA.  NCPA encourages CMS to apply lessons learned 
from PA modernization to future expansions to avoid replicating fragmentation.  
 
Pharmacists Should Be Able to Initiate and Submit PA 
Lastly, NCPA argues that nothing in existing or future CMS rules should prevent a pharmacist, 
enrolled as a provider if and when CMS allows pharmacists to enroll as providers, from initiating 
or submitting PA when they have access to the required information in the pharmacy’s records 
or accessed through the healthtech ecosystem. 
 
 
 
 
8 of 8 
 
 
Conclusion   
NCPA supports the proposed adoption of the NCPDP SCRIPT, F&B, and RTPB standards and 
emphasizes the importance of preserving their intended scope, promoting alignment across 
programs, and allowing adequate time for implementation. We appreciate CMS’ commitment to 
increasing interoperability and reducing administrative burden. 
NCPA appreciates the opportunity to share with CMS our comments and suggestions. Please let 
us know how we can assist further, and should you have any questions or concerns, please feel 
free to contact me at steve.postal@ncpa.org or (703) 600-1178. 
  
Sincerely,  
  
 
Steve Postal, JD 
Senior Director, Policy & Regulatory Affairs  
National Community Pharmacists Association

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA); signed by Steve Postal, JD, Senior Director, Policy & Regulatory Affairs.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; PBMs & Pharmacies; small business/community pharmacy representative.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents 18,900 independent community pharmacies, including many long-term care pharmacies; members employ 235,000 individuals and provide pharmacy and clinical services.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

NCPA supports CMS's proposal to require NCPDP Formulary & Benefit v60, RTPB v13, and SCRIPT 2023011 for pharmacy-benefit drug prior authorization, but urges CMS not to mandate newer NCPDP versions in the final rule. NCPA asks CMS to extend the pharmacy-benefit compliance date to no earlier than 24 months after the final rule effective date, clarify the medical-vs-pharmacy benefit pathway, define actionable workflow responses and PA clock rules, and ensure pharmacists can participate in and initiate prior authorization workflows where appropriate.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; GENERAL/RFIs; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 45 CFR 170.205(b), 45 CFR 170.205(c), 45 CFR 170.205(u); references to CMS-0057-F and CMS-0056-F.
- **Standards referenced:** NCPDP SCRIPT Standard Version 2023011; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit Standard Version 60; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit Standard Version 13; FHIR-based APIs; Da Vinci implementation guides; payer-to-payer APIs; ADT/event notifications.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: NCPDP standards and version adoption**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** NCPA supports adoption of the proposed NCPDP standards but says the industry is already transitioning to the named versions for Part D and is not prepared for a subsequent version mandate.
- **Specific request:** Finalize no NCPDP versions newer than SCRIPT 2023011, F&B v60, and RTPB v13.

**Topic 2: Pharmacy benefit implementation timeline**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** For non-Part D Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP payers, NCPDP SCRIPT ePA is net-new functionality requiring integrations, trading partner onboarding, testing, training, and operational changes.
- **Specific request:** Extend the October 1, 2027 pharmacy-benefit compliance date to no earlier than 24 months after the final rule effective date.

**Topic 3: Medical vs pharmacy benefit pathway clarity**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** CMS proposes two separate pathways, but pharmacists and other stakeholders need to know which pathway applies and receive actionable next steps to avoid misrouting, duplicate submissions, delays, and administrative burden.
- **Specific request:** Clarify payer expectations for identifying the correct authorization pathway, producing actionable responses, and orchestrating workflows across FHIR and NCPDP processes.

**Topic 4: Real-time benefit information and workflow integration**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Plan-level formulary files and real-time benefit responses are not operationally interchangeable; real-time responses should reflect adjudication processes that produce the same patient cost-sharing or utilization management determination as pharmacy claims.
- **Specific request:** Clarify expectations for actionable, patient-specific benefit information in workflows and ensure modernization produces workflow outcomes rather than merely endpoints.

**Topic 5: PA timeframes and the operational clock**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Without clear rules for when a request is received, complete, stopped, corrected, or rerouted, public reporting may misstate operational performance and shift accountability to pharmacists who do not control documentation completeness.
- **Specific request:** Define when the PA clock starts and stops, how incomplete requests are handled, and how iterative workflows, appeals, and peer-to-peer reviews should be treated.

**Topic 6: Pharmacist role and patient participation**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Pharmacists may be downstream dispensers who depend on prescriber documentation, but also may be clinical service providers responsible for documentation and submission.
- **Specific request:** Recognize pharmacists' dual role, include pharmacists as participants in real-time benefit and PA workflows, and do not prevent pharmacists from initiating or submitting PA when they are enrolled providers and have the required information.

**Topic 7: RFIs on event notifications, cybersecurity, API testing, step therapy, and lab/DMEPOS**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** NCPA supports broader interoperability improvements but warns that small community pharmacies have different infrastructure than large systems and that step therapy and lab/DMEPOS workflows can create fragmentation.
- **Specific request:** Include pharmacists in event-notification policy, account for small pharmacy cybersecurity capacity, strengthen API usability/testing, support step-therapy history portability, and apply PA modernization lessons to lab/DMEPOS.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S2/S60-S65:** Supports the proposed standards versions and advises CMS not to name newer NCPDP versions because the industry is already transitioning to the proposed versions.
- **S14/S19/S22:** Supports NCPDP standards for non-Part D impacted payers but states implementation is net-new and costly for Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP payers.
- **S21/S25/S31:** Requests a longer timeline for pharmacy benefit requirements and emphasizes RTPB/F&B operational differences.
- **S15:** Requests clarity on routing between medical-benefit FHIR workflows and pharmacy-benefit NCPDP workflows.
- **S20/S43:** Requests specificity on when PA timing clocks start, stop, and pause for incomplete, corrected, or rerouted requests.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Encourages CMS to make API and PA workflow measures meaningful and not merely endpoint-availability measures.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on event notifications, resiliency/cybersecurity, API testing and certification, step therapy, and lab/DMEPOS, with emphasis on pharmacist-enabled coordination and small-pharmacy feasibility.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize NCPDP SCRIPT 2023011, F&B v60, and RTPB v13, but do not mandate newer versions in this final rule.
2. Extend the pharmacy-benefit drug PA compliance date to at least 24 months after the final rule effective date.
3. Clarify how payers identify and communicate the correct medical-benefit vs pharmacy-benefit pathway.
4. Define what constitutes an actionable PA or benefit response.
5. Clarify the PA clock, including receipt, completeness, additional-information requests, corrected submissions, and rerouting.
6. Recognize pharmacists' dual dispenser/provider roles in PA workflows.
7. Ensure real-time benefit information is patient-specific and consistent with pharmacy claims adjudication.
8. Support patient visibility and appropriate patient participation in PA workflows without adding administrative burden.
9. Allow pharmacists to initiate or submit PA when they are enrolled providers and have necessary information.
10. Use RFIs to incorporate pharmacists in ADT/event notifications, step therapy portability, and future lab/DMEPOS PA modernization.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Premature version mandates; insufficient implementation time; disconnected FHIR and NCPDP workflows; unclear PA clock rules; lack of pharmacist-specific workflow recognition.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Administrative burden, misrouted requests, duplicative submissions, delayed access to medications, inaccurate reporting, and downstream accountability placed on pharmacists.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** New integrations, trading partner onboarding, testing protocols, staff training, fragmented multi-vendor ecosystem, small pharmacy infrastructure limitations, and overlapping CMS/HHS transaction mandates.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** NCPA represents 18,900 independent community pharmacies; nearly half provide long-term care services; members employ 235,000 individuals.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Cites Federal Register rule publication and CMS electronic prior authorization pledge/use case materials.
- **Examples provided:** Part D standards transition dates; need to avoid implementing SCRIPT 2017071 when 2023011 becomes required; pharmacist roles as both downstream dispenser and provider of clinical services.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Community and LTC pharmacies, pharmacists, Medicaid/CHIP and QHP payers, providers, patients, PBMs, vendors, and care teams.
- **Economic implications:** New version or rushed implementation mandates would impose administrative burden and cost on pharmacies and other stakeholders.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if CMS preserves proposed versions, extends timeline, and clarifies interoperable workflow routing and actionable responses.
- **Patient care impact:** Properly implemented real-time benefit and ePA workflows could reduce delays and improve medication access; poor routing or non-actionable responses could worsen delays.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with significant requested modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "NCPA supports this proposal." - Context: Support for NCPDP F&B v60 and RTPB v13 requirements.
2. "The industry is in active transition to the currently proposed versions and is not prepared for a subsequent version mandate." - Context: Version adoption recommendation.
3. "There is no existing infrastructure to update; it must be built." - Context: Implementation burden for non-Part D impacted payers.
4. "Absent additional clarity, there is risk that organizations implement parallel and uncoordinated workflows across FHIR and NCPDP standards." - Context: Need for medical/pharmacy pathway orchestration.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests at least 24 months after final rule effective date for pharmacy-benefit requirements.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Warns newer version mandates and net-new builds would create significant administrative burden and cost.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on pharmacy and provider workflow burden from misrouting and non-actionable responses.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Addresses cybersecurity/resiliency RFI and small pharmacy infrastructure limits.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Discusses integrations, testing, onboarding, and workflow orchestration feasibility.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Supports named NCPDP versions but opposes premature newer version mandates.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes immediate medication access and reducing PA delays.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for coordination across pharmacists, providers, payers, vendors, CMS, ONC, and NCPDP.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Central theme; requests clarity on routing between FHIR and NCPDP pathways.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests clear PA clock rules and actionable responses.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Addresses small community pharmacies rather than small payers, but the resource concern is analogous for smaller actors.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Emphasizes pharmacy claims adjudication, RTPB/F&B workflows, and pharmacist roles.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Notes fragmented multi-vendor ecosystem and trading partner onboarding.
